of  incessant  toil,  fatigue,  and  exposure  has  rarely  been  equaled  and 
never  excelled.  Kor  was  the  work  suspended  by  darkness.  On  either 
side  of  the  road  is  a  pitch-pine  forest,  or  turpentine  orchard,  which 
had  been  duly  tapped,  and  the  trees  being  lighted  furnished  long  lines 
of  illumination,  by  the  light  of  which  the  work  was  continued  during 
the  night  by  a  portion  of  the  command.  Having  extended  the  com¬ 
mand  several  miles  along  the  road,  corduroying  and  bridging.  Colonel 
Bertram’s  brigade,  being  in  advance,  at  length  reached  the  East  Fork  of 
Fish  Eiver.  I  ordered  him  to  push  on  to  Hannelly’s  Mills  with  his  bri¬ 
gade,  and  there  communicate  with  Major-General  Canby,  which  he  did* 
and  I  closely  followed,  with  the  Third  Division,  arriving  at  the  latter 
place  on  the  23d  of  March.  Two  brigades  crossed  the  river  and 
encamped  in  line  of  battle  on  the  right  of  the  Sixteenth  Army  Corps. 
My  First  Brigade  encamped  on  the  south  side  of  the  river.  At  this 
point  Colonel  Bertram,  pursuant  to  orders  from  the  corps  commander 
ceased  to  report  to  me.  March  25,  at  3  p.  m.,  my  division  moved  with 
the  army  toward  Spanish  Fort,  and  encamped  the  evening  of  the  26th 
near  the  enemy’s  works,  in  line  of  battle,  and  threw  up  temporarv 
defenses.  x  i  j 

On  the  morning  of  the  27th,  pursuant  to  orders  from  the  corps  com¬ 
mander,  I  moved  my  division  forward  in  column  of  brigades,  right  in 
front,  the  brigades  being  in  column  of  regiments.  I  held  the  right  of 
the  Thirteenth  Army  Corps,  connecting  with  Brigadier- General  Yeatch, 
First  Division,  Thirteenth  Army  Corps,  on  my  left,  and  with  the  Six- 
:eenth  Army  Corps  on  my  right.  Arriving  near  tlie  enemy’s  works  I 
ound  Brigadier-General  Slack’s  brigade,  of  the  First  Division,  fortify- 
ng  their  line  in  a  portion  of  my  front.  I  moved  my  division  forward 
through  Brigadier-General  Slack’s  brigade,  and  passing  his  works, 
leployed  my  division  in  plain  view  and  within  half  a  mile  of  the 
memy’s  works.  Colonel  Grier,  commanding  First  Brigade,  by  my 
iirection  deployed  a  regiment  as  skirmishers,  who  found  the  enemy’s 
skirmishers  immediately  in  my  front,  and  promptly  drove  them  to  the 
jover  of  their  rifle-pits,  near  their  works.  My  batteries  were  advanced 
;o  commanding  positions  upon  spurs  extending  toward  the  enemy,  and 
vere,  I  believe,  the  first  to  open  fire  upon  him.  By  my  orders  they 
fept  up  a  steady  and  well-directed  fire  during  the  day,  and  at  2  p.  m. 
vere  advanced  to  the  positions  they  afterward  held  during  the  entire 
siege.  My  division  was  also  advanced  to  within  a  few  hundred  yards 
fl  the  works  to  the  position  held  by  its  main  line  until  the  evacuation, 
ind  nearer,  I  believe,  than  any  other  troops  approached  that  day,  and 
vith  comparatively  very  few  casualties.  My  line  as  finally  established 
vas  by  inversion  of  brigades.  My  division  promptly  covered  its  front 
jy  works  of  considerable  strength,  my  skirmish  line  was  advanced 
luring  the  night,  and  my  batteries  strengthened. 

The  history  of  the  operations  of  my  command  from  this  time  until 
ne  evacuation  of  the  enemy  shows  a  sleepless  vigilance,  a  routine  of 
ucessant  toil  in  the  trenches  night  and  day,  a  gradual  and  sure 
pproach  to  the  enemy’s  works  by  means  of  the  pick  and  spade,  the 
Jgging  of  saps  and  parallels,  the  construction  of  batteries,  making  of

overcome,  and  the  want  of  sufficient  tools  at  the  commencement,  my

siege  howitzers,  and  mortars  were  constructed  by  the  labor  of  my 
division.  Late  in  the  afternoon  of  the  31st  of  March  the  enemy,  cov¬ 
ered  by  the  smoke  of  the  burning  brush  in  front  of  our  lines,  made  a 
sortie  and  succeeded  in  capturing  1  officer  and  22  enlisted  men  of  the

short  time  one  of  my  advanced  rifle-pits,  but  soon  after  dark  the  line 
was  retaken  at  the  point  of  the  bayonet,  and  afterward  held  by  our  men.

Reports  of  Col.  William  0.  Holbrook,  Seventh  Vermont  Infantry,  of  oper- 
ations  March  17-April  17. 

Hdqe-s  Seventh  Vermont  Veteran  Volunteers, 

In  the  Field,  near  AIoMle,  Ala.,  April  17,  1865. 

General  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  part  taken  by  my  regi¬ 
ment  in  the  siege  of  Spanish  Fort,  Ala.,  near  Mobile,  . 

The  regiment  left  Mobile  Point  March  17,  and  arrived  before  Spanish 
Fort  on  the  morning  of  March  27,  1865.  The  division  to  which  the 
regiment  is  attached  (Third  Division,  Thirteenth  Army  Corps)  was 
massed  and  moved  forward  to  within  about  500  yards  of  the  rebel  works, 
driving  back  the  enemy’s  skirmishers  as  it  advanced.  The  line  was 
here  halted,  and  we  remained  in  this  position  during  the  day,  sutr 
iected  to  a  heavy  fire  of  artillery  and  musketry.  At  night-fall  a  Ime  ot 
works  was  commenced,  and  during  the  night  we  moved  into  the 
trenches.  The  regiment  daily  furnished  one  or  two  companies  toi 
the  skirmish  line.  The  advance  rifle-pits  were  within  a  few  yards 
of  the  rebel  works.  Those  held  by  this  regiment  were  exposed  to  an 
incessant  flank  fire  from  the  enemy’s  artillery.  Captain  Stearns  and 
21  men  of  Company  K  were  captured  in  these  pits.  The  enemy  s  shells 
had  compelled  his  supports  to  fall  back,  and  had  set  fire  to  the  grass 
and  fallen  timber  in  his  rear,  enveloping  the  entire  line  in  a  dense  cloud 
of  smoke.  Captain  Stearns,  however,  maintained  his  position.  About 
dark  the  rebels  made  a  sortie,  capturing  him  and  21  of  his  nien.  Dur¬ 
ing  the  last  days  of  the  siege  the  regiment  assisted  in  putting  the 
siege  guns  into  position  and  making  approaches.  In  this  perilous 
oiieration  several  were  wounded.  The  regiment  has  in  every  instance 
done  excellently  well,  and  both  officers  and  men  have  behaved  witl 
great  gallantry. 

*  *  *  *  *  *. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  general,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient 

W.  C.  HOLBKOOK, 

Colonel  Seventh  Vermont  Veteran  Volunteers. 

Peter  T.  Washburn, 

Adjutant  and  Inspector  General,  State  of  Vermont.

General:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  part  taken  by  my  con 
mand  in  the  operations  around  Mobile,  which  resulted  in  the  captui 
of  Spanish  Fort  and  Blakely:  ,  , 

The  corps  having  been  concentrated  at  Dannelly’s  Mills,  the  head  < 
navigation  on  the  North  Branch  of  Fish  Fiver,  on  the  morning  of  tl 
25th  of  March,  the  command  moved  forward  northwest  by  north,  mei 
acing  both  Spanish  Fort  and  Blakely.  Continuing  the  march  on  tl 
26th,  with  some  slight  skirmishing  we  reached  Sibley’s  Mills,  a  poii 
on  Minette  Creek  four  miles  from  Spanish  Fort  and  about  seve, 
miles  from  Blakely.  On  the  morning  of  the  27th,  in  obedience  Ij 
instructions  from  Major-General  Canby,  the  Second  Division  of  n 
command,  Brig.  Gen.  K.  Garrard  commanding,  was  left  at  this  poii 
in  an  intrenched  camp  covering  the  Blakely  road  where  it  cross* 
Minette  Creek,  in  charge  of  tne  supply  trains  of  the  corps.  With  t 
First  and  Third  Divisions  of  the  corps,  I  moved  southwest  of  SpauL 
Fort,  driving  the  enemy’s  skirmishers  and  pickets  inside  then  wort

On  mv  left  was  Eeed’s  battery  5  on  the  left  of  this  still,  the  Second 
Brigade.  Directly  in  my  front  in  the  enemy’s  line  of  works  were  three 
bastion  forts,  the  center  one  of  which  afterward  becanie  known  as  the 
Bed  Fort,  all  strong  earth- works,  containing  guns  of  keavy  caliber. 
The  intervening  ground  was  nearly  level,  covered  with  faben  timber, 
and  a  line  of  abatis  formed  by  the  tops  of  trees.  During  tke  mght  of 
the  27th  ultimo  my  front  line  was  moved  up  to  within  about  500  j^ards 
of  the  enemy’s  works,  and  before  morning  the  men  were  covered  by  a 
good  rifle-pit,  thrown  up  during  the  night.  The  next  day  was  occupied 
in  strengthening  the  main  line  and  in  throwing  up  defensive  works  in 
the  various  camps.  On  the  evening  of  the  29th  ultimo  I  commenced  a 
sap  from  near  my  left,  which  was  pushed  with  vigor  until  within  about 
150  yards  of  the  enemy’s  works,  where  a  parallel  was  constructed  cover¬ 
ing  my  front  proper  in  the  main  line,  and  that  of  Feed  s  battery,  con¬ 
necting  on  the  left  with  a  similar  work  of  the  Second  Bripde.  Con¬ 
tinuing  my  sap  to  the  front  a  short  distance  farther,  I  6ug  ^<^1^ 
parall&  for  the  right  of  my  line,  which  threw  it  considerably  in  adyance 
of  the  Third  Division,  and  with  which  they  did  not  succeed  in  connect¬ 
ing  at  any  time  during  the  siege.  In  these  parallels  strong  bodies  of 
sharpshooters  and  pickets  were  constantly  kept  on  duty,  and  at  night 
skirmishers  were  thrown  out  and  advanced  as  far  as  possible  in  order 
to  hold  the  ground  and  cover  working  parties.  I  continued  my  sap 
toward  the  Bed  Fort  until  I  reached  a  point  some  sixty  or  seventy 
vards  from  it,  where  on  the  morning  of  the  7th  instant  I  commenced 
digging  another  parallel.  This  brought  my  sharpshooters  and  skirmish¬ 
ers  into  close  quarters  with  those  of  the  enemy,  and  a  skap  fire  was 
kept  up  by  both  sides.  I  was  engaged  on  this  work  until  ^he  night  ot 
the  8th  instant,  when  about  midnight  hearing  accidentally  that  the 
right  of  the  Third  Division  had  turned  the  enemy’s  left  flank  ancl  were 
inside  his  works,  I  immediately  ordered  an  advance  of  the  skirmist 
line  and  the  men  in  the  rifle-pits,  but  on  reaching  the  enemy  s  works 
they  were  found  abandoned.  A  lieutenant  and  16  men  were  capturec 

on  the  enemy’s  picket-line.  .  ^  ^ 

In  all  the  duties  of  the  siege  commanding  officers  of  regiments  anc 
officers  and  men  generally  displayed  that  courage,  eiffiurance,  and  deter 
mination  which  always  leads  to  success.  To  the  officers  of  my  staff  . 
am  again  indebted  for  their  prompt  co-operation  and  faithful  discharg 
of  all  duties.  1  desire,  however,  to  call  particuto  attention  to  m:

continued  labor  day  and  night,  often  exposing  him  to  great  danger,  bu 
they  were  performed  with  courage,  fidelity,  and  energy,  as  his  woi 
will  testify,  they  being  nearer  those  of  the  enemy  than  any  others  aloii 
our  entire  line,  as  far  as  I  have  seen.  I  recommend  him  for  promotio 
as  captain  and  aide-de-camp.  I  am  also  indebted  to  Lieut.  Col.  L.  b 
Eaton,  Seventy- second  Ohio,  for  valuable  services  in  digging  my  saj

I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  this  command  embarked  on  steamer

Dhree  miles  and  put  up  another  line  of  works.  On  the  morning  of  the

gade,  arriving  in  front  of  Spanish  Fort  on  the  27th  at  10  a.  m.  :^ormed  a 
ine  and  advanced  about  three-quarters  of  a  mile,  when  we  found  we 
vere  in  the  rear  of  one  regiment  of  Third  Division.  I  then  moved  by 
eft  flank  until  we  unmasked,  then  by  the  right  flank  to  a  commanding 
losition  within  300  yards  of  the  strong  works  of  the  fort  and  proceeded 
o  erect  fortiflcations.  During  the  night  made  works  sufficient  to  ren-

Most  incessant  fire  of  the  enemy’s  artillery  and  musketry.  Frequently

to  state,  with  effect.  In  a  moment  the  rebel  skirmishers  commenced 

running.  ,  ,  . 

Colonel  Kinney  started  his  line  rapidly  forward ;  his  reserves  were 
ordered  out  to  support  his  skirmishers,  and  the  buglers  sounded  ‘‘for¬ 
ward.”  I  at  once  put  the  whole  line  out  on  double-quick,  knowing  that 
under  the  artillery  fire  of  grape  and  canister  which  was  opened  on  my 
skirmish  line  it  must  either  be  destroyed  or  go  into  the  fort;  and  from 
that  moment  the  whole  brigade  was,  with  a  shout,  going  over  the  faller 
trees,  tangled  vines  and  brush,  and  through  the  swamp  at  a  full  run, 
and  that  under  severe  and  rapid  fire  from  artillery  and  musketry.  Ir 
from  five  to  ten  minutes  from  the  advance  of  the  skirmish  line  the 
enemy’s  works  were  carried  and  the  national  flag  waved  oyer  them 
The  regiments  were  reformed  in  the  fort  as  soon  as  possible  aftei 
entering  it,  and  the  trophies  and  wounded  which  belonged  to  the  com 
mand  looked  after  and  taken  care  of.  Among  the  trophies  were  4  rebe 
battle-flags,  3  of  which  were  captured  by  the  One  hundred  and  nine 
teenth  Illinois  Yolunteer  Infantry,  and  1  by  the  One  hundred  an( 
twenty -second  Illinois  Yolunteer  Infantry;  10  pieces  of  artillery  and  . 
mortars.  There  were  a  great  many  small-arms,  much  ammunition,  am 
some  wagons  and  mules  fell  into  our  hands  when  we  entered  the  works 
We  captured  520  prisoners,  37  commissioned  officers,  among  whom  wer 
2  brigadier-generals,  viz,  General  Thomas  and  General  Liddell,  th 
latter  of  whom  was  in  command  of  the  fort  and  rebel  -forces,  48' 
enlisted  men.  The  casualties  iu  the  brigade  during  the  charge  were 
in  all,  14  killed  and  46  wounded.  During  whole  siege  and  assault,  1 
killed  and  54  wounded.  Too  much  praise  cannot  be  given  Col.  Thoina 
J  Kinney  for  the  gallant,  able,  and  efficient  manner  in  which  he  an 
his  whole  duty  in  the  gallant  charge  with  his  skirmish  line  over  tli 
rebel  works  on  the  9th  instant,  which  kept  as  well  in  advpce  as  tliei 
physical  strength  permitted  them  to  do.  Each  of  the  regimental  con 
manders  did  well  their  whole  duty,  as  did  also  the  line  officers  and  me 
of  the  several  regiments.  All  rushed  forward  and  entered  the  work 
almost  simultaneously  with  the  skirmishers.  Lieutenant- Colonel  Drisl 
One  hundred  and  twenty-second  Illinois,  fell  severely  wounded  jin 
before  reaching  the  first  line  of  abatis,  and  the  command  of  the  reg 
ment  devolving  upon  Maj.  J.  F.  Chapman,  he  gallantly  led  it  on. 
also  take  pleasure  in  stating  that  my  staff  officers  did  their  respectiv 
duties  well.  Lieutenant  McLean,  who  was  immediately  with  me  i 
starting  the  troops  forward  from  the  rifle-pits,  behaved  with  gret 
bravery.  But  to  particularize  where  all  did  their  duty  well,  were  invia

les  of  the  First  Florida.  He  had  driven  the  enemy’s  pickets  toward 
ard,  and  was  holding  the  place  for  the  purpose  of  concealing  the

column.  In  order  further  to  deceive  the  enemy  he  was  instructed 
>emain  at  Milton  until  the  column  had  left  Creigler’s  Mills,  then  to 
IS  the  river  at  noon  and  overtake  the  force  as  soon  as  practicable, 
direct  route  to  Andalusia,  Ala.,  was  taken.  The  early  part  of  the 
was  rainy  and  uncomfortable.  The  brooks  and  creeks  were  swollen 
j.he  constant  ram.  During  the  whole  day  the  march  was  through  a 
•  y  country ,  and  notwithstanding  the  bad  weather  the  roads  were  in 
condition.  Nothing  of  importance  occurred  during  the  march  of

inff  me  a  warm  reception.  It  was  thouglit  that  I  would  reach  the  place 
on  the  evening  of  the  23cl.  At  4  o’clock  in  the  morning  the  march  was 
resumed,  and  at  5.30  o’clock  I  reached  Andalusia.  No  resistance 
was  made  whatever.  I  caused  all  the  arms  and  ammunition  that  could 
be  found  in  the  place  to  be  destroyed.  The  people  were  generally  armed 
with  the  Enfield  musket.  What  little  property  belonged  to  the  rebel 
Government,  and  could  be  found,  was  destroyed.  I  left  the  place  at  8i 
a  m.  and  marched  toward  Evergreen.  Met  with  no  opposition  during 
the  day,  but  at  night  a  little  after  dark,  and  when  six  miles  from  Ever-, 
green,  I  came  suddenly  upon  three  rebels.  They  atteinpted  to  escape 
and  two  of  them  were  wounded  and  all  were  made  prisoners.  One  oi 
them  (wounded)  proved  to  be  a  Lieutenant  Wyatts,  of  General  Clanton’s 
staff,  and  a  son  of  Governor  Watts.  A  little  before  midnight  I  reached 
the  Alabama  and  Florida  Kailroad  at  a  point  five  miles  above  Ever¬ 
green.  I  immediately  caused  the  telegraph  wires  to  be  cut  and  the  rail-, 
road  track  to  be  torn  up.  At  4.30  a.  m.  March  24  the  train  of  cars  from 
Pollard  came  up  the  road.  It  was  thrown  from  the  track,  set  on  fire, 
and  destroyed.  It  consisted  of  1  locomotive,  1  baggage,  2  passenger,  and 
4  platform-cars.  At  7  o’clock  the  train  arrived  from  Montgomery  and  was 
captured  and  destroyed;  100  soldiers,  including  7  commissioned  officers 
were  captured  on  this  train.  Their  destination  was  Mobile.  The  trail 
consisted  of  1  locomotive,  1  baggage,  4  passenger,  and  2  freight  cars,, 
There  was  considerable  corn,  clothing,  &c.,  in  the  cars,  all  of  which  was^ 
destroyed.  Having  captured  and  destroyed  both  trains  of  cars,  I  pro 
ceeded  with  my  force  to  Evergreen,  where  I  arrived  at  11  a.  m.  Hen, 
I  obtained  an  abundance  of  forage  and  rations  and  destroyed  som( 
stores.  What  little  rolling-stock  was  found  at  the  station  was  burned 
I  left  Evergreen  at  2  p.  m.  en  route  for  Sparta.  I  reached  the  statioi 
at  4  o’clock.  All  the  rolling-stock— six  box-cars— was  destroyed.  Som( 
quite  important  trestle-work  on  the  road  was  burned,  and  the  depot 
filled  with  stores  and  warlike  material.  The  command  went  into  camj 
for  the  night  at  Sparta. 

March  25,  the  column  moved  at  5  a.  m.  on  the  road  leading  to  ErooK 
lyn,  which  place  was  reached  at  11.30  o’clock.  The  march  was  con 
tinned  till  sundown,  when  a  halt  was  made  twelve  miles  from  Brewtoi 
Station.  I  reached  Brewton  Station  at  11  a.  m.  on  the  following  day 
I  found  that  a  part  of  the  planking  of  the  bridge  across  Muddji 
Creek  had  been  removed,  and  it  would  be  necessary  to  repair  tm 
bridge  before  my  force  could  cross.  I  sent  over  an  advance  guar( 
(dismounted)  to  see  if  they  could  find  any  enemy.  The  rebels  s^i 
opened  fire  from  behind  a  small  breast-work  and  then  ran  away.  AVi| 
were  not  able  to  capture  them.  Lieutenant  Mose,  of  the  Second  Mai^ 
and  two  enlisted  men  of  that  regiment  were  slightly  wounded.  Th 
bridge  was  repaired,  the  march  resumed,  and  continued  on  the  direc 
road  to  Pollard,  which  place  I  reached  with  my  command  at  6  p.  in 
Sunday,  March  26,  and  where  I  learned  of  the  success  and  advance  o> 
the  army.  The  results  of  the  expedition  in  the  way  of  prisoners,  cap: 
tured  property,  &c.,  which  I  have  with  me,  are  120  prisoners,  20 
negroes,  250  horses  and  mules.  The  conduct  of  officers  and  men  wa 
at  all  times  good.  I  do  not  deem  it  necessary  to  make  special  mentio 
of  auy  one  where  all  have  done  their  duty  equally  well. 

I  am,  captain,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

A.  B.  SPURLING, 

Lieutenant- Colonel  Seeond  Maine  Cavalry^  Commanding. 

Capt.  John  E.  Lacey,

Pursuant  to  orders  received  the  evening  of  the  31st  of  March,  the 
cond  Brigade  left  Stockton  at  5  a.  m.  April  1,  for  the  purpose  of  open- 
^  communication  with  and  joining  the  U.  S.  forces  operating  against 
naiiish  Fort  below  Blakely.  When  within  seven  miles  of  Blakely 
li^  advance  guard  came  in  contact  with  the  enemy’s  picket;  four  of

stance  farther  on  other  pickets  were  captured  and  one  mortally 
Dunded.  Five  miles  from  Blakely  1  came  upon  the  enemy  in  force, 
living  satisfied  myself  that  there  was  no  other  route  by  which  I  could 
t  through  to  communicate  with  Major-General  Canby,  unless  I 
traced  my  march  for  many  miles,  I  concluded  to  fight.  The  Second 
line  Cavalry  was  dismounted  and  deployed  on  each  side  of  the  road 
fight  on  foot.  This  regiment  was  moved  forward  under  a  brisk  fire, 
lich  was  as  briskly  returned.  The  enemy  slowly  retired  before  this 
1  vance,  taking  shelter  behind  fences  and  everything  that  could  afford 
iotection.  They  retired  in  this  way  for  over  a  mile,  contesting  every 
3h  of  the  ground.  I  had  moved  the  Second  Illinois  up  the  road,  and 
pt  its  advance  on  a  line  with  the  Second  Maine,  and  judging  that  the 
vorable  opportunity  had  arrived  I  charged  the  enemy  with  that  regi- 
mt.  It  was  a  complete  success.  His  whole  force  was  routed  and  a 
rtion  of  it  captured.  Two  companies  of  the  Second  Illinois  Cavalry 
rsued  the  fugitives  within  half  a  mile  of  the  enemy’s  works  at 
akely,  from  which  a  sharp  fire  was  opened  with  artillery.  In  all,  74 
m  were  taken  prisoners,  including  3  commissioned  officers.  I^early 
[[  of  them  were  members  of  the  Forty-sixth  Mississippi  Infantry, 
le  colors  of  that  regiment  were  also  captured;  8  horses  and  mules 
)re  taken;  70  stand  of  arms  captured  and  destroyed.  The  casualties 
ire:  One  mortally  wounded.  He  was  so  near  to  the  enemy’s  works 
at  he  could  not  be  brought  off  by  his  comrades.  One  man  slightly 
Dunded  in  the  foot  by  the  explosion  of  a  torpedo.  Both  of  these  men 
longed  to  the  Second  Illinois  Cavalry.  Four  horses  of  that  regiment 
,ire  killed.  After  I  had  whipped  the  enemy  and  driven  him  into  his 
Tifications  at  Blakely  I  got  my  force  into  a  good  position  to  halt, 
id,  &c.,  when  the  main  column  came  up.

I  have  the  honor  to  inform  the  general  commanding  that  I  made  a 
out  this  morning  in  the  direction  of  Stockton.  I  had  with  me  for  the 
casion  about  thirty  men,  all  well  mounted.  When  eight  miles  from 
mp,  I  received  information  that  a  small  squad  of  rebel  cavalry  was 
the  immediate  vicinity,  and  must  be  in  close  proximity  to  me.  I  soon 
scovered  them  drawn  up  in  a  cross-road.  They  were  routed,  1  of 
eir  number  killed  and  2  severely  wounded.  I  pursued  the  fugitives 
r  a  long  distance.  Mne  rebels  in  all  were  made  prisoners;  all  their 
ms,  equipments,  &c.,  were  captured,  and  the  arms  were  destroyed.

Eight  horses  were  also  captured.  Among  the  prisoners  were  two  com

their  escape.

over  Kew  Eiver  had  been  disabled  by  cutting  away  two  be_nts.  Ine 
iron  and  cross-ties  for  twenty  miles  east  of  the  bridge  were  destroyed,

depot  of  commissary,  quartermaster’s,  and  ordnance  supplies,  amon^ 
which  were  a  large  amount  of  ammunition  and  10,000  pounds  of  powder 
and  that  in  compliance  with  his  instructions  he  had  recrossed  tlie 
Eiver  at  Porter’s  Ferry  and  awaited  further  orders.  Colonel  Millei 
reported  that  he  had  been  attacked  by  the  enemy  with  infantry  am 
cavalry  at  Wytheville,  but  had  repulsed  them,  and  mthdrew  with  { 
loss  of  thirty-five  men  killed,  wounded,  and  missing.  He  was  directe(

the  direction  of  Jacksonville,  at  which  place  we  arrived  at  10  a.  ir

1  officer  killed  and  5  men  wounded. 

On  the  10th  we  moved  south,  arriving  at  Germantown  at  12  m.  in 
number  of  negroes  who  were  following  the  column  had  increased  to  sue 
an  extent  as  to  endanger  the  safety  of  the  command  in  case  it  shou

General  Orders,  )  Hdqrs.  Fourth  Div.,  Oav.  Corps, 

>  Military  Division  of  the  Mississippi, 

21.  )  Edgefield,  Tenn.,  June  10,  1865. 

Before  severing  liis  connection  with  the  command,  the  brevet  Diajor- 
general  commanding  desires  to  express  liis  liigli  appreciation  of  the 
teavery,  endurance,  and  soldierly  qualities  displayed  by  the  officers  and 
men  of  his  division  in  the  late  cavalry  campaign.  Leaving  Chickasaw 
on  the  22d  of  March  as  a  new  organization  and  without  status  in  tne 
Cavalry  Corps,  you  in  one  month  traversed  600  miles ;  crossed  six  rivers; 
met  and  defeated  the  enemy  at  Montevallo,  capturing  100  prisoners; 
routed  Forrest,  Buford,  and  Eoddey  in  their  chosen  position  at  Eben- 
ezer  Church,  capturing  2  guns  and  300  prisoners;  carried  the  wOTks  m 
your  front  at  Selma,  capturing  13  guns,  1,100  ® 

flnffs  and  finallv  crowned  your  successes  by  a  night  assault  upon  the 
enemy’s  intrenchments  at  Columbus,  where  you  captured  1,500  prisoners, 
21  guns,  8  battle-flags,  and  vast  munitions  of  war.  April  21  you  arrived 
at  Macon,  having  captured  on  your  march  3,000  prisoners,  39  pieces  oi 
artillery,  and  13  battle-flags.  Whether  mounted  with  the  saber  oi  d» 
mounted  with  the  carbine,  the  brave  men  of  the  Third,  Fourth,  auji 
Fifth  Iowa,  First  and  Seventh  Ohio,  and  Tenth  Missouri  Cavalry  tri 
umphed  over  the  enemy  in  every  conflict.  With  regiments  led 
brave  colonels  and  brigades  commanded  with  consummate  skill  anc 
daring,  the  division  in  thirty  days  won  a  reputation  unsurpassed  in  the 
service  Though  many  of  you  have  not  received  the  rewards  your  gal 
lantry  has  entitled  you  to,  you  have  received  the  commendation  of  yom 
superior  officers  and  have  won  the  admiration  and  gratitude  of  youi 
countrymen.  You  will  return  to  your  homes  with  the  proud  conscious 
ness  of  having  defended  the  flag  of  your  country  in  the  hour  of  th. 
greatest  national  peril,  while  through  your  instrumentality  liberty  auc 
civilization  will  have  advanced  the  greatest  stride  recorded  m  history 
The  best  wishes  of  your  commanding  general  wdlCTer  attend  you. 

E.  U F J-O-M , 

By  JAMES  W.  LATTA, 
Assistant  Adjutant- General.

liad  been  checked  and  was  being  gradually  forced  back.  Explosions 
of  shell  still  continued.  Captain  Owen,  acting  quartermaster,  has 
lost  all  his  stores  j  forage  burnt.  Some  horses  and  mules  are  reported 
to  have  broken  loose  and  are  saved.  Of  the  immediate  cause  of  the 
explosion  there  are  none  to  tell.  Captain  Beebe’s  employes  in  charge 
of  the  stores  state  that  ammunition  was  being  transferred  from  the 
railroad  to  the  warehouse  by  a  detail  of  colored  troops.  A  lieutenant 
commanding  the  squad  at  the  warehouse,  and  having  more  men  than 
he  could  use  at  the  time,  allowed  the  idle  men  to  lounge  in  the  ware¬ 
house  about  the  ammunition.  He  was  admonished  of  the  danger,  but 
to  no  purpose.  The  employe  then  procured  an  order  from  the  captain 
of  the  company  for  the  lieutenant  to  send  him  twenty  men,  the  surplus 
and  upon  returning  found  the  lieutenant  absent  and  the  men  still  more 
reckless.  On  leaving  the  warehouse  the  lieutenant  was  found  on  board 
the  steamer  Kate  Hale  and  the  order  delivered.  The  employe  then  left, 
and  when  two  or  three  blocks  ofi:’  the  explosion  occurred.  The  report 
that  it  is  the  work  of  an  incendiary  receives  little  credit.  It  is  reported 
that  paroled  prisoners  quartered  near  have  suiiered  severely.  The  fire 
appears  [to]  extend  over  about  two  acres  and  a  half  and  there  are  about 
SIX  acres  of  ruined  buildings.  The  whole  northeast  quarter  of  the  city 
has  a  dilapidated  appearance.  The  windows  and  ceiling  of  the  custom¬ 
house  shattered.  Killed  and  wounded  probably  500,  which,  with  the 
severe  loss  of  property  to  the  army,  cannot  yet  be  estimated  properly. 
All  officers  are  actively  engaged.  The  ruins  are  covered  with  dense 
smoke.  I  send  map  inclosed.* 

I  am,  colonel,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

JAS.  G.  PATTOK, 

Captain  and  Acting  Assistant  Inspector- General.

dureau  is  to  establish  its  depots  for  recuperation  at  such  points,  which,

'eadily  obtained.  The  remounts  after  being  assembled  at  these  points

)0ssible,  instead  of  sending  the  troops  for  them.  While  we  are  at  this

Major-General  Thomas: 


Pulaski,  [January]  26 ^  1865, 


Dispatch  of  22d  just  received.*  Before  you  left  Nashville  I  had  sent 
the  Eighth  Michigan,  via  Murfreesborough,  Shelbyville,  and  Fay¬ 
etteville,  to  this  place,  with  orders  to  scout  the  country  thoroughly. 
This  regiment  arrived  here  a;  few  days  since.  Previous  to  its  arrival 
I  had  only  about  200  mounted  men,  the  Sixteenth  Illinois,  General  Wil¬ 
son  having  taken  from  me  two  mounted  regiments,  leaving  me  a  force 
entirely  inadequate  for  my  purpose.  I  shall  send  a  regiment  toward 
New  Market  and  Salem  on  the  27th.  By  that  time  I  will  have  had 
elothing  issued,  of  which  the  •men  are  in  need.  I  have  not  heard  of  a 
guerrilla  west  of  this  place,  though  I  will  send  out  the  remaining 
mounted  force  in  that  direction.  A  single  courier  arrived  yesterday 
from  General  Wilson’s  headquarters,  and  trains  without  escort  and 
^mall  parties  have  been  passing  almost  every  day  without  beinff 
nolested.  ^ 


E.  W.  JOHNSON, 
Brigadier-  General.

II.  Colonel  Mix,  Eighth  Michigan  Cavalry,  will  march  with  his  regi- 
nent  on  Saturday  at  daylight,  the  28th  instant,  for  Fayetteville.  At  Fay- 
‘tteville  he  will  be  joined  by  200  men  of  the  Fifth  Tennessee  Cavalry 
narching  from  Shelbyville.  This  detachment  is  ordered  to  be  here  by 
:  p.  m.  Colonel  Mix  will  unite  this  force  with  his  own,  and  will  then 
>atrol  the  country  in  the  neighborhood  of  Fayetteville,  New  Market, 
nd  Winchester,  and  the  triangle  of  country  embraced  between  these 
mints.  He  is  expected  to  clear  this  country  of  guerrillas  and  such 
traggling  parties  of  Confederate  cavalry  as  may  be  found  there,  and 
nil  govern  his  operations  by  what  information  he  can  from  time  to 
ime  obtain  from  citizens  or  any  other  source,  bearing  in  mind  that 
7hat  is  desired  is  not  the  mere  dispersion  of  those  forces,  but  to  cap- 
are  or  kill  them,  and,  if  guerrillas,  they  are  not  to  be  captured.  He 
nil  take  with  him  as  much  bread,  sugar,  coffee,  and  salt  as  the  men 
an  carry  without  too  much  encumbering  the  horses.  The  country 
mst  be  relied  upon  for  rations  when  this  gives  out.  All  serviceable 
orses,  and  none  but  serviceable  horses,  will  be  impressed.  Colonel 
I ix  must  see  that  in  all  cases  receipts  are  given  for  property  taken 
pecifying  whether  the  owner  is  loyal  or  disloyal.  Indiscriminate  pil- 
ige  must  not  be  permitted.  Except  one  ambulance,  no  wheels  will 
ccompany  the  regiment. 

HI.  Lieut.  Col.  E.  W.  Smith,  commanding  Sixteenth  Illinois  Cavalry, 
nl  detach  a  force  of  seventy  men  or  thereabouts  from  his  regiment 
nd  send  them  in  command  of  an  efficient  and  reliable  officer  to  Law- 
nieeburg,  thence  to  Lexington,  and  thence  crossing  the  country  to  the 
m  to  Sugar  Creek,  thence  returning  to  this  point.  The  command 
111  carry  bread,  sugar,  salt,  and  coffee  for  five  days.  They  must  depend 
pon  the  country  for  meat  rations.  No  wheels  will  accompany  the

ispatch  is  required  I  advise  their  marching  to  Eastport.  It  is  not 
mch  over  100  miles  and  only  four  feet  of  water  on  shoals  and  falling

hs  message  to  commanding  officer  of  Fourth  Corps,  so  that  he  may

Captain:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report  on  the  con- 
ition  of  the  defenses  of  this  city :  The  length  of  line  is  ten  miles  and 
quarter,  extending  from  Eeargrass  Cut  Off,  on  the  east,  where  it 
npties  into  the  Ohio,  to  the  mouth  of  Upper  Paddy’s  Euu,  on  the 
est.  It  IS  to  be  defended  by  eleven  forts  and  twelve  batteries.  Ten  of 
le  form^  are  nearly  finished,  and  two  batteries  commenced.  Except 
ort  McPherson,  the  main  works  are  redoubts  of  from  550  to  700  feet 
3velopment  of  crest,  and  intended  to  mount  from  four  to  six  guns 
id  on  an  average  the  minimum  garrison  of  each  will  be  200  infantry 
Id  50  artillery,  the  maximum,  three  times  that  number.  Minimum 
irnson  for  the  ten  redoubts  of  main  works  2,000  infantry,  500  artil- 
ry ;  Fort  McPherson,  500  infantry,  1 00  artillery.  Total,  2,500  infantry, 
to  artillery.  In  addition,  there  are  to  be  between  each  of  the  main 
rts  one  or  two  batteries  (see  tracing).*  These  are  to  be  manned  by 
ovable  light  artillery,  12-pounder  smooth-bores  preferable.  Three  or 
ur  such  batteries  to  be  stationed  at  central  points,  to  move  where 
quired.  There  should  also  be  an  infantry  force  as  large  as  can  be 
id  distributed,  part  in  rifle-pits  (to  be  dug  by  themselves)  near  the 
term^iate  batteries,  the  rest  as  reserves  at  central  points  in  the 
ar.  The  batteries  are  to  be  a  short  distance  in  rear  of  line  connect- 
g  adjacent  forts.  They  will  average  200  feet  development,  and  are 
liilt  in  the  same  manner  as  the  forts,  with  plank  revetments,  platforms 
d  embrasures,  but  without  magazines,  and  of  sufficient  command  to

Washington,  D.  0.,  February  4, 1865. 

Major-General  Thomas, 

Eastport : 

The  order  was  to  send  about  5,000  cavalry,  not  five  divisions.  Both 
Smith  and  the  cavalry  must  have  their  transportation,  but  we  want 
Smith’s  infantry  sent  as  quickly  as  possible  to  Canby  to  assist  at  Mobile. 
The  transportation  which  they  cannot  conveniently  take  along  can  fol¬ 
low  as  well  as  the  cavalry  and  artillery.  Would  it  be  convenient  to 
!iave  Memphis  and  all  West  Tennessee  added  to  your  department, 
leaving  the  troops  there  subject  as  now  to  be  moved  by  General  Oanby’s 
irders,  if  required,  down  the  river  or  on  west  side?  The  present 
lepartment  lines  are  inconvenient,  and  yet  it  seems  important  that  all 
posts  on  the  river  should  be  under  one  command,  in  order  to  prevent 
Kirby  Smith  from  crossing. 

H.  W.  HALLECK, 
Major-General  and  Chief  of  Staff.

General:  I  inclose  herewith  a  report  showing  the  number  of  horses 
required  to  mount  all  the  men  of  tlie  four  divisions  now  here.  Tne  hirst 
Division  requires  1,000,  but  500  of  this  number  will  be  supplied  from 
recuperation  of  horses  now  on  hand.  The  other  500  are  for  men  now 
daily  expected  to  arrive,  recruits,  convalescents,  &c.  The  Second 
Division  requires  720  for  men  who  have  joined  since  the  command  lett 
Louisville.  Horses  sufficient  for  the  Fourth  Division  have  just  arrived 
in  charge  of  Winslow’s  brigade,  so  that  500  horses  will  actually  supply 
all  deficiencies.  Be  good  enough  to  lay  this  before  tlm  major-general 
commanding,  and  ask  him  to  solicit  the  attention  ot  General  Halleck 
to  the  necessity  of  furnishing  the  horses  at  once.  M  itli  one  thorough 
remount  and  an  ordinarily  successful  campaign,  1  think  I  can  keep  the 
corps  mounted  without  cost  to  the  Government.

Barrancas.  Fla..  February  14,  1S65. 

laj.  Gen.  E.  E.  S.  Canby, 

Neiv  Orleans: 

Dear  General:  On  Sunday  I  sent  you  notes  of  an  examination  of 
hree  deserters  from  the  Sixth  Alabama  Cavalry,  stationed  at  Canoe 
Itation.  The  same  evening  I  examined  two  colored  men  who  had  just 
ome  in  from  Montgomery.  They  formerly  lived  at  New  Orleans,' but 
oon  after  the  war  commenced  were  taken  by  their  mistress  to  Sparta, 
here  they  have  lived  for  the  past  three  years  and  till  within  a  few 
reeks,  when  they  were  sent  to  Montgomery  to  work  on  fortifications, 
'hey  say  there  are  about  200  colored  men  making  fortifications  on  the 
orth  side  of  Montgomery,  and  think  there  are  about  4,000  infantry 
liere,  and  do  not  know  but  there  are  more.  They  thought  they  noticed 
wo  gun-boats  on  the  river  at  that  place.  They  made  their  escape  and 
ame  down  via  Brooklyn  and  Blackwater  Eiver.  In  the  neighborhood 
f  Brooklyn,  and  between  that  place  and  Sparta,  they  say  there  is  an 
bundance  of  corn  and  cattle;  also,  that  six  miles  below  Brooklyn,  on 
be  Conecuh  Eiver,  a  home  guard  of  fifty  men  are  watching  a  bridge, 
^hich  they  have  prepared  to  burn  on  the  approach  of  the  Yankees,  whom 
ley  have  expected  from  the  direction  of  Milton.  Sergeant  Hollinger,of 
irst  Florida  Cavalry,  who  was  raised  near  Little  Eiver,  describes  a  route 
om  here  to  Blakely  which  avoids  difficult  streams,  striking  the  rail- 
lad  at  Williams  Station,  six  miles  below  Canoe  Station ;  thence  north- 
est,  intersecting  Stockton  road;  thence  southwest  to  Blakely, leaving

people  who  are  timid  about  their  persons  and  property,  and  ‘

recruits  from  the  ranks  of  this  class  that  we  may  hope  eventually  t< 
control  the  State  against  the  secessionists.  If  I  understand  the  polit

guerrillas,  with  every  prospect  of  soon  breaking  up  and  driving  on 
the  outlaws.  If  taken  from  me  I  have  no  troops  with  which  to  i  eplac

regret  exceedingly  the  probable  removal  of  the  Twelfth  Kentucky  Cav¬ 
alry  from  my  command,  as  great  pains  have  been  taken  to  put  this

from  guerrilla  outrages.  I  do  not  doubt  the  jiropriety  of  nw  superior 
olhcers  in  removing  troops  under  my  command  from  their  present  sta-

iltville  m  October,  1864,  is  incorrect.  I  have  ascertained  what  troops

eutenant  Smith  at  Emory  and  Henry  Hospitals  by  Champ  Ferguson 
IS  one  of  the  most  diabolical  acts  committed  during  the  war,  and  I 
1  surprised  at  its  being  passed  over  without  notice  by  the  Confed- 
ite  authorities.  Should  he  or  any  of  the  band  that  accompanied  him 
this  occasion  fall  into  the  hands  of  TJ.  S.  forces  they  will  not  be

Major  :  A  deserter  who  left  Hood’s  army  at  Montgomery,  Ala.,  on 
3 16th  instant  reports  that  army  had  all  gone  to  Branchville  except 
3  division  of  Stewart’s  corps,  which  was  at  Mobile.  The  last  division 
Cheatham’s  corps  left  Selma,  Ala.,  two  weeks  ago  to-day.  Lee’s  and 
swart’s  corps  had  left  about  ten  days  before.  He  estimated  the  entire 
ce  at  18,000  to  20,000.  He  had  received  a  furlough  to  return  when 
eatham’s  corps  train  arrives  at  Augusta,  Ga.

Mai.  G.  M.  Bascom, 

Assistant  Adjutant- General : 

Guerrilla  squads  have  appeared  in  Owen  and  Carroll  Counties.  Have 
strengtliened  my  recruiting  parties  in  that  direction.  A  band  crossed 
the  pike  near  Georgetown  on  Saturday  and  robbed  mail  carrier.  Three 
night  attacks  are  reported  at  i^ew  Haven  on  detachment  of  Sixth  U.  b. 
Colored  Cavalry.  Have  sent  Colonel  Armstrong,  with  another  com¬ 
pany,  to  that  place  with  orders  to  drive  out  the  guerrillas,  occupy 
Bloomfield,  and  recruit.  Have  armed  200  colored  recruits  at  this  place.

tain  Bennett,  at  others  Major  Jones  or  Magruder.  For  a  long  tiuH 
they  have  not  gone  east  of  the  point  mentioned  on  Obey  River.  Geii, 
erally  on  their  return  to  Obey  River  they  bring  goods  ot  various  kiiicl 
and  hide  them  away  among  the  hills.  Yesterday  I  had  a  long  convei 
sation  with  H.  D.  Johnson,  of  Overton.  I  know  he  is  in  communicatioi 
with  Hughes,  Gatewood,  and  others.  He  has  a  son  with  the  rel.n 
Colonel  Dibrell,  formerly  of  Sparta.  Johnson  says  the  rebels  will  b. 
in  this  section  of  country  in  considerable  force  late  in  the  spring,  c, 
so  soon  as  it  shall  seem  the  rivers  will  not  rise  suddenly  and  reimn 
full  any  length  of  time.  There  is  the  same  old  evil  disposition  amon, 
the  rebels,  the  same  hate,  but  they  fear  more  and  hide.  It  any  oUj 
doubts,  let  him  become  for  a  time  a  rebel  and  go  among  them,  where  b| 
is  not  known  to  be  other  than  what  he  seems. 

Very  respectfully,  j.  D.  HALE.

nen  in  Mobile,  and  that  he  witnessed  a  review  of  them.  It  is  reported 
hat  there  are  two  heavily  fortified  bluffs  on  the  Alabama  River;  also 
hat  Selma  is  well  fortified.  The  inhabitants  of  Mobile  expect  it  to  be 
aken,  but  not  without  a  fight;  it  will  not  be  evacuated.  The  two

disgraceful,  bringing  discredit  not  only  upon  themselves  and  the  regi¬ 
ments  to  which  they  belong,  but  also  unnecessary  seizure  of  horses  and 
property  of  all  kinds,  and  by  the  unwarranted  abuse  of  good  citizens. 
These  are  positively  forbidden,  and  can  not  and  will  not  be  tolera  •

Barrancas^  March  4,  1865. 

Brig.  Gen.  John  P.  Hawkins, 

Commanding  First  Division^  U.  S.  Colored  Troops : 

General  :  In  regard  to  your  desire  that  the  Twenty-fifth  and 
Eighty^sixth  U.  b.  Colored  Infantry  Eegiments  be  relieved^from  duty 
and  ordered  to  report  to  you  at  the  camp  of  your  division,  I  beg  leave 
to  give  the  fohowiug  explanation;  First.  Special  Orders,  No.  54,  head- 
quarters  Military  Division  of  West  Mississipiii,  dated  February  23 
giving  the  number  of  regiments  intended  for  the  organization  of  your 
division  comprises  in  the  First  Brigade  three  regiments  stationed  here 
for  the  last  year,  namely,  the  Twenty-fifth,  the  Eighty-second,  and  the 
Eighty-sixth  Regiments.  Second.  The  Twenty-fifth  Regiment  is  garri- 
^ning  Fort  Pickens,  Barrancas,  the  redoubt,  and  guarding  Gun-boat 
Point,  at  the  mouth  of  the  Bayou  Grande  above  the  navy- yard.  The 
Eighty-second  and  Eighty-sixth  are  busily  engaged  in  completing  the 
line  ot  fortifications  between  the  beach  and  Fort  Barrancas,  Barrancas 
and  redoubt,  and  redoubt  and  Bayou  Grande,  and  it  is  important  that 
this  work  IS  done  before  the  troops  take  the  field.  Third.  I  have  no 
other  troops  at  my  disposal  to  relieve  with  and  replace  these  three 
regiments  in  the  several  forts  and  on  the  line  of  fortifications.  Fourth 
I  have  received  no  orders  to  relieve  those  three  regiments  from  duty 
with  this  district,  which  would  leave  all  the  forts  without  garrison,  and 
prevent  the  completion  of  the  line  of  fortifications. 

Under  these  embarrassing  circumstances  I  consider  it  the  best  expe- 
dient  that  these  regiments  continue  to  remain  at  their  present  duties, 
and  that  the  Seventy-third  U.  S.  Colored  Infantry,  just  arrived  be 
encamped  near  the  Eighty-second  and  Eighty-sixth,  in  order  to  have 
the  regiments  of  the  h  irst  Brigade  of  your  division  united  as  much  as 
possible  preparatory  to  their  taking  the  field.  I  feel  inclined,  general, 

arnlJiTf  these  my  views,  pending  the  daily  expected 

arrival  of  Major-General  Oanby,  commanding,  and  his  final  orders  in 
me  matter. 

Very  respectfully,  general,  your  obedient  servant, 

ASBOTH, 

Brigadier- Genera^  Commanding.

Tullahoma,  March  7, 1865, 

Maj.  Gen.  G.  H.  Thomas: 

I  have  here  in  arrest  two  noted  rebel  women,  Mrs.  Dolly  Battle  and 
MlssSallie  Battle,  who  reside  ten  miles  from  Nashville,  but  came  all 
the  way  to  Wartrace.  on  horseback,  two  days  ago,  to  recoffin  and  bury 
the  body  of  Trummei,  alias  Van  Houghton,  who  was  killed  at  that 
nlaceon  the  night  of  the  21st  ultimo,  while  engaged,  with  nine  other 
guerrillas,  in  robbing  the  telegraph  office  and  stores.  The  daguerreo¬ 
types  of  these  two  she  rebels  were  found  on  the  body  of  this  robber 
tffi-ef  after  he  was  killed,  with  letters  from  them  showing  great  intimacy. 
They  boast  that  they  are  rebels  and  have  never  taken  the  oath,  iheir 
father  is  an  officer  in  the  rebel  array;  their  brother  Bob  is  a  guerrilla. 
This  family  haye  been  spies  and  harborers  of  rebels  and  guerrillas  since 
the  beginning  of  the  war.  Their  mother,  as  I  was  weU  iiffioriued  last 
summer,  boasts  that  they  have  done  more  good  for  the  Confederate 
cause  than  a  regiment  of  soldiers.  I  respectfully  ask  permission  to 
send  these  two  south  of  our  lines.  ^  ^  MIBEOY 

Major- General.

Chief  of  Staff: 

For  the  last  forty  days  we  have  had  but  seven  of  favorable  weather. 
During  all  the  rest  of  this  time  heavy  easterly  and  southeasterly  gaies

and  dense  fop  have  prevailed,  rendering  the  transportation  of  troops 
and  ppphes  both  tedious  and  dangerous.  Some  material  has  been  loS 
but  fortunpely  no  hves.  Twelve  sound  steamers  selected  for  service  in 
Mississippi  Sound  and  Mobile  Bay  have  been  at  the  Passes  of  the  Mis- 
sipippi  since  the  26th  ultimo,  but  have  been  unable  to  cross  the  bar 
These  stpmers  are  capable  of  carrying  10,000  men,  and  two  days  of 
fair  weather  will  enable  us  to  bring  over  from  New  Orleans  evervthinp- 
exppt  the  cavalry.  About  half  of  the  Sixteenth  Corps  is  now  here 
and  the  remainder  will  arrive  within  the  next  two  days.  Only  a  small 
ppt  of  the  cavalry  has  been  brought  over,  but  it  will  arrive  in  season 
The  navy  will  not  be  ready  for  several  days,  but  our  movements  for 
getting  into  position  for  co-operation  will  go  on  at  once.

General  Orders,  ')  Headquarters  Second  Division, 

[  Thirteenth  Army  Corps, 

)  Barrancas,  Fla.,  March  10,  1865. 

I.  To  make  successful  marches  in  the  enemy’s  country  requires  zeal 

activity,  and  watchfulness  on  the  part  of  every  officer,  ^ 

II.  Officers  will  re-examine  and,  as  far  as  practicable,  adhere  to  what 
lollows  under  the  head  of  marches,  convoys,  and  their  escorts  and 
camps,  in  the  Eevised  Army  Regulations. 

III.  Officers  will  have  their  commands  in  such  readiness  as  to  avoid 

hurry,  confusion,  and  extra  fatigue,  both  of  men  and  animals,  iust 
before  starting.  ^ 

ly.  On  a  march  the  men  will  not  be  called  up  earlier  than  one  hour 
before  marching,  but  the  cooks  will  have  breakfast  in  readiness  imme¬ 
diately  after  reveille.  Wood  will  be  jirepared  the  night  previous.  If 
necessary,  in  the  artillery  the  men  will  be  called  up  one  hour  and  a 
half  before  marching. 

y.  As  a  general  rule  troops  should  march  at  daylight.  Every  com- 
aaand  will  be  ready  to  move  at  the  time  specified.  Neglect  on  the  part 
if  a  very  few  sometimes  delays  and  annoys  a  whole  column.  Those 
Aerefore,  who  are  guilty  of  neglect  and  tardiness  in  this  respect  will 
neet  with  rigorous  and  severe  punishment.  No  matter  what  the 
veather  is,  there  can  be  no  excuse  for  tardiness.  Commanding  officers 
vill  every  evening  ascertain  the  standard  time  for  the  column. 

yi.  The  order  of  march  will  be  announced  daily.  Brigades  will  gen¬ 
erally  alternate  as  the  advance  and  rear,  and  regiments  will  alternate 
IS  the  advance  and  rear  guard.  Rear  and  advance  guards  will  keep 
)ut  patrols  or  scouts  (to  be  frequently  relieved)  and  should  never  suffer 
i  surprise. 

yil.  Generally  there  will  be  a  halt  of  ten  minutes  each  hour.  These 
lalts  will  be  regulated  by  the  general  commanding  the  division 
he  sipal  of  attention”  by  the  bugle  will  precede  the  signal  for 
halt,”  and  also  the  signal  for  forward.”  These  commands  will  be 
peated  along  the  column  verbally,  or  by  a  roll  of  the  drum  or  note  of 
he  bugle.  The  major  or  senior  officer  at  the  rear  of  the  leading  regi- 
oent  will  ppeat  the  commands  so  that  they  may  be  heard  at  the  head 
it  the  regiment,  battalion,  or  battery  next  in  the  rear, 
yill.  No  man  will  leave  the  ranks  without  the  permission  of  the 
ommandmg  officer  of  his  company,  and  such  leave  will  not  be  granted 
TV  necessity.  Neither  officers  nor  men  will  enter  houses. 

IX.  Th^e  general  commanding  trusts  that  there  is  not  a  man  in  the 
ivision  but  will  disdain  to  commit  an  act  of  plunder.  He  will  not  be 
urprised  to  learn  that  the  heroic  and  generous  men  of  his  command 
ave,  in  some  instances,  out  of  their  own  scanty  fare,  fed  the  poor  and 
uiigry  along  their  routes,  but  will  be  surprised  to  learn  that  any  one 
t  them  has  done  an  act  unbecoming  to  the  humanity  and  the  proud 
haractp  of  an  American  soldier. 

X.  Where  the  country  affords  it,  all  necessary  subsistence  will  be 
aken  under  existing  orders  in  a  regular  manner,  so  as  to  be  issued  to 
ae  troops  equally. 

i  XI.  The  music  will  play  occasionally  to  enliven  the  march,  and  each 
B^ment  and  battalion  will  march  into  camp  with  its  band  playing. 

XII.  Immediately  after  arriving  in  camp  there  will  be  a  roll-call  of 
^ery  company,  and  immediately  thereafter  regimental  commanders 
'111  lorward  through  brigade  headquarters  a  report  of  the  result, 
mating  the  number  absent  in  each  company,  the  names  of  the  missing 
i*  who  have  absented  themselves  during  the  day,  and  the  name  of 
leir  captain  or  company  commander.

iiiirN  L-N., 


XIII  The  hour  for  tattoo  ■will  be  fixed  daily.  The  signal  for  taps  i 
•will  be’quarter  of  an  hour  after  tattoo,  after  -which  perfect  silence  -will  i 
1)G  observed* 

XIV.  At  night  a  camp  or  alarm  guard  will  be  on  duty  in  each  regi 
ment  or  battalion,  the  sentinels  to  be  relieved  at  least  every  hour. 

XV.  All  commissioned  officers  will  give  their  peponal  attention  to  th( 
enforcement  of  what  is  prescribed  above.  They  will  anticipate  neglects 
and  by  reasonable  and  prudent  efforts  prevent  their  occurrence.

II.  The  district  within  the  department  thus  thrown  open  to  trade 
shall  be  bounded  as  follows : 

On  the  north,  by  a  line  drawn  from  Fort  Henry,  on  the  Tennessee 
Ri^/er,  to  Fort  Honelson,  on  the  Cumberland;  thence  up  the  Cumber¬ 
land,  as  far  as  the  boundary  of  the  Department  of  the  Ohio,  or  to  the 
mouth  of  Caiiey  Fork ;  thence  up  the  Caney  Fork  to  Sparta;  thence  in  a 
southeasterly  direction  to  Washington,  on  the  Tennessee  River;  thence 
down  the  Tennessee  to  the  point  of  starting,  and  including  Chattanooga 
and  Cleveland. 

The  points  within  the  above-described  district  at  which  trade  may 
be  opened  are  Nashville,  Columbia,  Franklin,  Pulaski,  Chattanooga, 
Cleveland,  Decherd,  Shelbyville,  Winchester,  McMinnville,  and  Mur- 
freesborough,  Tenn. ;  Athens,  Decatur,  Huntsville,  and  Stevenson,  Ala. 

III.  The  value  of  the  stock  of  goods  to  be  permitted  for  each  of  the 
above-named  places,  or  such  other  places  as  supply  stores  may  be  opened 
at,  shall  be  such  as  may  be  agreed  upon  by  the  post,  district,  or  depart¬ 
ment  commander,  and  the  supervising  special  agent  of  the  Treasury. 

IV.  For  the  sale  of  articles  not  coming  within  the  meaning  of  this 
order,  permits  will  be  required  from  these  headquarters. 

V.  Purveyors  at  the  headquarters  of  the  different  corps,  divisions, 
and  brigades  of  this  army,  will  be  permitted  to  bring  to  the  army  articles 
for  the  use  of  the  officers  and  soldiers  serving  at  such  headquarters, 
upon  special  permits  to  be  renewed  each  month,  approved  by  the  gen¬ 
eral  commanding  the  corps,  division,  or  brigade,  and  in  quantities  not 
to  exceed  in  value  for  each  month,  $800  for  the  headquarters  of  a  brigade, 
$1,000  for  a  division,  and  $1,500  for  the  headquarters  of  a  corps.

Brigade  commanders  will  call  in  all  safeguards,  commencing  with 
the  most  remote  from  camp.  Preparations  will  be  made  to  break  up 
the  division  hospital,  the  sick  to  be  disposed  of  as  directed  by  the 
medical  director  of  the  corps.  The  tents  and  stores  will  be  ready  for 
shinment  by  rail.  Ordnance  trains  will  be  unloaded  and  the  stores 
shipped  by  rail.  Trains  will  leave  here  loaded  with  seven  days’  forage 
and  ten  days’  rations  for  one  regiment  to  be  detailed  as  train  guard. 
In  the  approaching  movement  of  the  division  the  horses  of  mounted 
officers  and  pack  animals  authorized  by  General  Orders,  No.  1,  head¬ 
quarters  Fourth  Army  Corps,  January  12,  1865,  except  those  of  one 
regiment  to  be  detailed  hereafter  as  train  guard,  will  be  shipped  by 
rail  with  the  troops.  Detailed  instructions  as  to  the  time  of  movement 
will  be  given  hereafter.

Hdqrs.  Cavalry  Corps,  Mil.  Div.  of  the  Mississippi, 

Gravelly  Springs,  A  la.,  March  12,  186 j. 

Brig.  Gen.  E.  Hatch, 

Commanding  Fifth  Division,  Cavalry  Corps: 

General:  Your  letter  of  tlie  10th  is  just  received.  Whatever  you 
determine  to  do  in  the  matter  of  arms  will  be  entirely  satisfactory  to 
me;  but  as  a  matter  of  course  it  is  not  expected  in  any  case  that  you 
will  disarm  your  command  or  any  part  of  it  without  replacing  their 
arms  with  others  of  some  kind  to  do  until  the  new  Spencers  can  be 
obtained.  Your  disposition  of  the  horse  question  is  equally  satistac- 
tory.  I  have  written  to  Chambliss  at  Louisville,  requesting  him  to  do 
all  in  his  power  toward  furnishing  you  with  a  complete  and  good  rent, 
sending  everything  to  Eastport  if  possible,  and  as  fast  as  may  be.  i 
am  anxious  to  have  you  get  ready  for  the  field  without  going  back,  for 
if  you  once  get  to  Kashville  or  Huntsville  there  will  be  a  great  tempta¬ 
tion  to  detach  you  to  hunt  guerrillas  and  separate  y^  from  the  corps. 
1  am  more  than  anxious  to  prevent  this  if  possible.  Fearing,  however, 
that  everything  in  the  way  of  cavalry  supplies  would  be  diverted  from 
us,  I  have  written  to  Chambliss  requesting  him  to  fill  up  all  his  stables 
with  the  best  of  his  recuperated  stock  and  have  them  set  aside  for  you. 
Since  I  saw  you  Major  Price  has  written  me,  saying  he  would  spare  no 
efforts  to  put  your  division  on  the  best  war  footing  the  latest  improve¬ 
ments  would  permit.  You  will  therefore  in  all  probability  have  a  long 
rest;  but  I  am  sure  you  will  do  all  in  your  power  to  expedite  matteis 
and  make  the  command  all  that  either  of  us  could  desire.  I  am  veiy 
much  obliged  to  you  for  the  willingness  you  manifest  to  put  the  marcU 
ing  divisions  in  good  condition  by  stripping  yourself.  I  am  sorry, 
however,  that  the  short-sighted  policy  of  parties  responsible  for  it  ha. 
prevented  us  from  having  enough  of  everything  needed  the  entire 
command.  Please  make  every  effort  to  keep  me  informed  of  rebe 
movements  in  Northern  Alabama  and  Mississippi.  Canby’s  movemeni 
from  Vicksburg  has  been  abandoned  because  of  the  heavy  rains 
Everything  will  go  from  the  Gulf  coast.  Please  direct  Chaplain  De 
to  visit  me  here  before  he  leaves  for  Illinois.  He  belongs  to  the  Sixtl 
Illinois  Cavalry. 

Yours,  very  respectfully,  ^  WILSON, 

Brevet  Major- General.

General  Orders,  )  Hdqrs.  Department  of  Kentucky, 

^  Louisville^  Ky.,  March  12^  1865. 

The  general  commanding  announces  to  the  colored  men  of  Kentucky 
that  by  an  act  of  Congress  passed  on  the  3d  day  of  Alarch,  1865,  the 
wives  and  children  of  all  colored  men  avIio  have  heretofore  enlisted,  or 
who  may  hereafter  enlist,  in  the  military  service  of  the  Government, 

are  made  free.  ^  i  4. 

This  act  of  iustice  to  the  soldiers  claims  from  them  renewed  eliorts, 
bv  courage,  fortitude,  and  discipline,  to  win  a  good  name,  to  be  shared 
bv  a  free  wife  and  free  children.  To  colored  men  not  in  the  army  it 
ofrers  an  opportunity  to  coin  freedom  for  themselves  and  posterity. 

The  rights  secured  to  colored  soldiers  under  this  law  will,  if  neces¬ 
sary,  be  enforced  by  the  military  authorities  of  this  department,  and  it 
is  expected  that  the  loyal  men  and  women  of  Kentucky  will  encourage 
colored  men  to  enlist  in  the  army;  and,  after  they  have  done  so,  recog¬ 
nize  them  as  upholders  of  their  Government  and  defenders  of  their 
homes,  and  exercise  toward  the  helpless  women  and  children  made  free 
by  law  that  benevolence  and  charity  which  has  always  characterized 
the  people  of  the  State. 

By  command  of  Alajor-General  Palmer:  ^  p  WATSOK 

Cajyiain  and  Acting  Assistant  Adjutant- General.

Colonel:  I  have  the  honor  to  submit  to  your  consideration  the  fol- 
Dwing  report  of  information  received  at  this  office  this  loth  day  of 
larch,  1865:  In  Selma  there  is  one  arsenal,  one  naval  ordnance  works, 
en  iron  foundries,  eight  machine-shops,  one  shovel  factory,  one  card 
ictory  for  carding  cotton,  two  wagon  factories,  and  one  horseshoe  fac- 
ory.  There  is  also  a  large  rolling-mill  in  operation.  Selma  is  the 
epot  for  all  the  iron  and  coal  that  is  distributed  through  Georgia, 
».labama,  and  Mississipiii,  the  coal  and  iron  mines  being  only  forty  five 
files  above,  on  the  Alabama  and  Tennessee  Eailroad,  at  Montevallo. 
he  stage  road  to  Montgomery  from  Selma  is  fifty-eight  miles,  and  is 
ood.  There  are  three  bridges  on  it  of  a  very  primitive  style.  The 
ailroad  from  Selma  to  Demopolis,  sixty  miles  distant,  is  in  good  order: 
•om  Demopolis  to  Meridian  it  is  very  bad,  scarcely  fit  to  travel  on. 
he  city  of  Selma  is  fortified  on  three  sides  with  palisades.  Fortifica- 
ons— they  are  not  worth  much,  for  about  a  mile  west  of  the  city  is  a 
ill,  which  an  invading  force  could  hold  and  command  the  city.  There 
re  not  200  troops  in  the  city,  as  they  expect  the  citizens  to  defend  the 
ity  in  case  of  an  attack.  There  are  seven  or  eight  iron  furnaces  in 
■ibb  County  from  forty  to  seventy  miles  above  Selma,  on  the  Tennessee 
ailroad.  Some  of  them  are  from  three  to  ten  miles  distant  from  the 
lad.  The  distance  from  Selma  to  Mobile  by  river  is  about  365  miles* 
lere  are  no  batteries  on  the  river.  There  were  fortifications  on  Choc- 
iw  Bluff,  but  the  guns  have  been  taken  away  and  the  place  is  now 
ismantled.  The  distance  to  Cahawba  from  Selma  by  the  wagon  road  is 
iu  miles,  and  is  very  bad.  There  were  700  Gnion  prisoners  confined

Invariably  there  will  be  kept  a  jcurnal  of  march  of  the  form  prescribed 
in  Army  Eegulations,  edition  1863,  page  99,  et  seq.,  except  that  the  col¬ 
umn  headed  Weather’^  will  be  headed  Bearings,”  and  will  contain  the 
magnetic  bearings  of  consecutive  portions  of  the  road,  anti  that  the  col¬ 
umn  of  distances  will  be  kept  in  yards  instead  of  miles.  A  convenient 
scale  is  five  minutes  between  two  consecutive  lines  of  ruled  letter  paper, 
which  corresponds  to  about  430  yards  passed  over  by  infantry.  This 
journal  will  contam  all  the  data  for  a  map  of  the  road  and  its  vicinity, 
so  clear  as  to  be  intelligible  to  others  besides  the  maker  and  to  admit 
of  being  platted  by  them.  The  remarks  will  contain  all  important  mili¬ 
tary  information  which  can  be  more  readily  noted  in  writing  than  in 
drawing.  The  more  important  topographical  features  are :  First,  rojids; 
second,  water  courses;  third,  means  of  crossing  water-courses;  fourth 
differences  of  level;  fifth,  woods,  and  sixth,  towns.  ^ 

1.  Roads. — State  their  kind,  as  shell,  plank,  corduroy,  soil,  &c. ;  their 
condition,  as  muddy,  miry,  sandy,  dusty,  &c.;  average  width,  whether 
flush  with  the  ground,  or  contracted  in  a  cutting  or  an  embankment  or 
between  woods  or  marshes,  &c. ;  whether  there  are  cross-roads  con¬ 
necting  them,  the  character  of  the  bordering  ground,  and,  if  cultivated, 
with  what  crops,  the  nearest  principal  places  on  both  sides  of  the  road 
on  the  cross  and  branch  roads;  if  lined  with  fences,  hedges,  ditches, 
levees,  &c. ;  sharp  turns ;  bad  places  needing  repairs  when  ikt  and  what 
sort,  &c. 

2.  T1  ater-courses. — State  their  width,  depth,  and  velocity  at  present 
stage  of  water,  at  low  water,  and  at  high  water;  whether  subject  to 
sudden  rises,  character  ot  bottom,  hard,  soft,  Quicksand,  &c. ;  nature 
of  banks,  steep  or  gentle  slope,  level  or  broken  ground,  grassy,  wooded; 
tidal  or  not;  fit  to  drink  or  not;  any  islands. 

3. ^  Means  of  crossing  water-conrses.—FixQd  bridges,  floating  bridges, 
fepies,  and  boats,  fords.  Necessity  for  repairs  and  fitness  for  passage 
ot  the  three  arms  when  left.  Nature  of  approaches,  as  hilly  or  level, 
broken  or  smooth,  wooded  or  open,  concave  or  convex,  which  bank 
commands  the  other  and  how  much,  &c. ;  how  best  destroyed  or 
replaced;  best  positions  for  new  ones  and  material  for  constructing 
them ;  how  to  be  fortified,  defended,  or  attacked.  If  a  bridge,  its 
length,  width,  and  height  above  surface  of  water;  nature,  as  piled, 
stone,  brick,  or  wood  arches,  trusses,  trestles,  &c.;  dimensions  of  piers, 
^idth  and  number  of  bays,  span,  rise,  and  thickness  of  arches,  &c. 
For  floating  bridges,  boats,  or  ferries,  time  of  passage  and  capacity  of 
transportation  for  one  trip,  for  each  arm,  separately  or  mixed;  how  and 
to  what  extent  this  allows  of  being  increased  and  means  available  for 
this.  For  fords,  the  form  and  nature  of  the  banks  at  each  end,  nature 
)f  bottom,  marks  and  directions  to  determine  the  path,  greatest  depth 
)f  water  and  where  situated;  whether  others  exist  and  where;  whether 
^hey  are  likely  to  become  suddenly  impassable. 

4.  Differences  of  level. — Highest  and  lowest  points  in  slopes  in  road, 

vith  approximate  difference.  Eminences  in  sight  on  either  side  of  road 
vithin  cannon  range,  with  approximate  height  above  nearest  point  of 
•oad.  Slopes  requiring  drag  chains  to  descend  or  increasing  teams  to 
iscend;  commanding  point  on  banks  for  covering  or  forcing  passage  of 
-treams;  advantageous  positions  for  batteries,  cuttings,  embankments, 
Qarshes,  prairies,  &c.  ;  ?  ? 

trees,  free  from  underbrush,  traversable  for 
rtillery,  cavalry,  or  infantry,  distance  from  the  road ;  whether  they  can 
>e  skirted;  are  there  houses  within  clearings;  if  so,  how  large;  is  the 
|3^und  level,  broken,  marshy,  cut  with  ravines  or  streams,  &c.;  nature

of  ground  around  tlie  woods,  &c.  To  reconnoiter  a  forest  tliorouglily

II.  Under  all  circumstances  these  notes  must  be  platted  at  the  end  i

used.  All  the  above  information  possible  will  be  given  by  topograph-  k

warded  in  a  clear,  concise  memoir,  written  on  letter  paper  in  a  definite, » 
exact,  condensed  style.  Three  copies  of  map  and  memoir  will  be  made,  i 
all  of  which  must  be  signed  by  division  engineer.  One  of  each  will  be 
retained  by  him  and  two  sent  that  day  to  the  corps  engineer,  one  of. 
them  to  be  forwarded  by  him  to  the  chief  engineer  of  the  army,  or  his 
chief  topographer,  and  the  other  retained.  Immediately  on  getting 
into  cam})  the  division  engineer  will  accompany  the  commander  of  his 
division  in  his  examination  of  his  front,  if  he  makes  one  immediately; 
if  not,  the  brigade  officer  posting  pickets,  and  give  all  necepary 
instructions  for  strengthening  and  intrenching  the  front  of  his  division, 
as  required  by  General  Field  Orders,  No.  1,  headquarters  Army  and 
Division  of  West  Mississippi.  After  this  he  will  examine  the  commu¬ 
nications  between  different  parts  of  his  division,  and  between  his; 
division  and  the  one  which  preceded  it  on  the  march,  and  make  the: 
necessary  arrangements  for  perfecting  these.  He  will  make  a  concise 
report  in  writing  to  the  corps  engineer  of  what  he  has  done,  with  such 
rough  sketch  as  may  be  necessary  to  explain  this.  When  absent  trom 
division  headquarters  he  will  leave  such  information  of  the  duty  and. 
locality  he  is  attending  to  as  will  enable  him  to  be  readily  found.. 
When  the  same  camp  is  occupied  two  days,  the  disposition  of  troops 
by  regiments  and  batteries  will  be  located  by  the  division  engineer  and 
duplicate  maps  sent  as  jiromptly  as  possible  to  the  corps  engineer.. 
When  on  the  march  the  pioneer  company  needs  attention  apart  from 
the  head  of  the  column,  either  the  division  engineer  or  Ins  assistant 
will  remain  with  it,  but  not  both.  The  other  will  go  on  and  keep  the 
notes  as  above.  When  necessary,  mounted  orderlies  and  escorts  will 
be  assigned  to  division  engineers  to  assist  them  in  obtaining  the  infor¬ 
mation  herein  specified,  or  to  carry  out  these  xmovisions.  Gomims- 
sioned  officers  may  also  be  ordered  to  reiiort  to  them  for  temporary 
duty  as  assistants.

Hdqrs.  Twenty-third  Iowa  Volunteer  Infantry, 

Mohile  Point,  Ala.,  March  15,  1865. 

Lieut.  A.  J.  Eockwell, 

Acting  Assistant  Adjutant- General,  First  Brigade: 

Lieutenant  :  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  in  obedience  to  Special 
Orders,  No.  20,  headquarters  First  Brigade,  Second  Division,  Thirteenth 
Army  Corps,  I  moved  from  the  camp  of  this  brigade  with  the  Twenty- 
third  Iowa  and  Twentieth  Wisconsin  and  a  detachment  of  scouts,  on  the 
13th  instant,  at  8  a.  m.,  and  arrived  at  Mr.  Childers’  farm,  twelve  miles 
distant,  at  12  m.  the  same  day,  where  I  halted  the  infantry  and  sent 
the  scouts  forward  to  Bon  Secours  Eiver.  From  Mr.  Childers’  farm  I 
moved  back  down  the  bay  to  Shell  Bank  and  camped  during  the  night. 
Steamers  even  of  light  draft  cannot  be  landed  at  Shell  Bank  or  any 
place  between  there  and  Bon  Secours  Eiver,  without  building  a  pier 
from  400  to  600  yards  in  length,  and  there  is  no  material  in  the  neigh- 
borliood  to  build  a  pier  with.  The  country  from  here  to  Mr.  Childers’ 
farm  is  thickly  interspersed  with  lagoons.  There  are  no  good  roads — 
nothing  but  narrow  and  crooked  paths.  I  met  no  enemy;  neither  could 
I  obtain  any  reliable  information  concerning  the  enemy  or  his  move¬ 
ments.  I  returned  to  camp  on  the  evening  of  the  14th  instant. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

’  S.  L.  GLASGOW, 

Colonel,  Commanding.

931 


West  Tennessee.  In  doing  so  it  is  due,  both  to  myself  and  the  troops 
thus  placed  under  my  command,  to  say  that  every  efiFort  will  be  made 
to  render  them  thoroughly  effective.  To  do  this,  strict  obedience  to  all 
orders  must  be  rigidly  enforced  by  subordinate  commanders,  and  imompt 
punishment  inflicted  for  all  violations  of  law  and  of  orders.  The  rights 
and  property  of  citizens  must  be  respected  and  protected,  and  the  ille¬ 
gal  organizations  of  cavalry  prowling  through  the  country  under 
various  authorities,  not  recognized  as  legitimate,  or  which  have  been  by 
the  proper  authorities  revoked,  must  be  placed  regularly  and  properly 
in  the  service  or  driven  from  the  country.  They  are  in  many  instances 
nothing  more  nor  less  than  roving  bands  of  deserters,  absentees,  strag¬ 
glers,  horse-thieves,  and  robbers,  who  consume  the  substance  and  anpro- 
priate  the  property  of  citizens  without  remuneration,  and  whose" acts 
of  lawlessness  and  crime  demand  a  remedy,  which  I  shall  not  hesitate 
to  apply,  even  to  extermination.  The  maxim  ^Hhat  kindness  to  bad 
men  is  cruelty  to  the  good,^’  is  peculiarly  applicable  to  soldiers,  for  all 
agree  that  Avithoiit  obedience  and  strict  discipline  troops  cannot  be 
made  effective,  and  kindness  to  a  bad  soldier  does  great  injustice  to 
those  who  are  faithful  and  true,  and  it  is  but  justice  to  those  who  dis¬ 
charge  their  duties  with  promptness  and  fidelity  that  others  who  are 
disobedient,  turbulent  and  mutinous,  or  avIio  desert  or  straggle  from 
their  commands,  should  be  promptly  and  effectively  dealt  with,  as  the 
law  directs.  I  sincerely  hope,  therefoi  e,  while  in  tlie  discharge  of  the 
arduous  duties  devolving  upon  me,  and  in  all  the  efforts  necessary  to 
render  the  troops  of  this  command  available  and  effective  to  suppress 
lawlessness  and  defend  the  country,  I  shall  have  the  hearty  co-oper¬ 
ation  of  all  subordinate  commanders,  and  the  unqualified  support  of 
every  brave  and  faithful  soldier.  • 

[N.  B.  FOEREST.]

commands  be  sent  up  to  this  place.  Major  Bennett  will  come  with  them 
also  the  quartermasters  of,  or  attached  to,  the  other  Tennessee  com¬ 
mands.  Send  their  ordnance  wagons  also,  but  let  all  their  wagons 
come  light  or  empty,  sending  everything  up  by  rail  to  this  place  that 
otherwise  would  be  brought  in  the  wagons.  Armstrong’s  brigade  is 
furloughed  until  the  10th  of  February,  to  meet  then  at  West  Point. 
The  major-general  commanding  directs  me  to  say  that  he  wishes  you  to 
get  up  all  the  Mississippi  commands  as  rapidly  as  possible,  as  they  will 
also  be  reorganized.  Let  the  officers  of  Gholson’s  command  be  sent 
with  details  in  such  numbers  and  such  directions  as  will  enable  them 
to  get  up  their  men,  to  report  with  same  at  least  by  the  10th,  and  all 
absentees  from  that  command  at  that  time  will  be  sent  to  infantry,  offi¬ 
cers  dropped  from  rolls  and  conscripted,  and  the  regiments  consolidated 
unless  they  are  filled  up.

[General  S.  Cooper  :]  '  | 

General:  In  accordance  with  instructions  from  the  Navy  Depart-  i 
ment,  communicated  to  me  by  Commodore  Earrand,  that  officer  trans¬ 
ferred  to  my  command  the  torpedo-boat  Saint  Patrick,  built  on  a  contract 
with  the  Government  by  a  man  named  Halligan.  This  boat  was  to 
have  been  ready  for  action  in  July  last,  and  I  hoped  to  use  it  against  i 
the  enemy’s  fleet  off  Fort  Morgan.  I  therefore  caused  every  possible! 
assistance  to  be  given  to  Halligan  in  building  her,  and  urged  her  early 

completion.  It  was  not,  however,  till  the  month  of -  Halligan 

arrived  here  with  the  boat,  and  from  his  whole  course  I  became  con-  • 
vinced  he  had  no  real  intention  of  attacking  the  enemy,  and  that  the 
only  practical  purpose  the  Saint  Patrick  was  serving  was  to  keep  Halli¬ 
gan  and  her  crew  of  six  able-bodied  men  from  doing  military  duty.  I 
therefore  had  him  supplied  with  every  means  to  move  against  the 
enemy,  and  notified  him  that  if  he  did  not  attack  at  once  I  would  place 
an  officer  in  charge  of  her  who  would.  In  the  course  of  a  few  days  I 
found  it  necessary  to  suiiersede  Halligan,  who  then  placed  his  affairs 
in  the  hands  of  a  lawyer  and  procured  from  Richmond  a  transfer  of  his 
boat  to  the  naval  commander  on  this  station.  Impressed  with  the 
importance  of  using  so  formidable  a  vessel  as  this  is  said  to  be,  I  have 
continually  and  repeatedly  urged  Commodore  Earrand  to  make  Halli¬ 
gan  attack  or  to  place  the  boat  in  charge  of  one  of  the  many  clever 
young  officers  of  the  navy  or  army  who  have  been  pressing  for  the  com-, 
mand  of  her.  This,  however,  he  did  not  do  until,  in  consequence,  I 
presume,  of  my  official  reports  to  higher  authority  he  was  ordered  to 
transfer  the  Saint  Patrick  tome.  I  immediately  asked  him  to  let  mehave 
Lieutenant  W alker,  of  the  navy,  to  command  her.  And  on  placing  that 
officer  in  charge  of  the  vessel,  now  lying  under  the  guns  of  the  eastern 
shore,  he  found  that  Halligan  had  been  absent  from  lier  for  two  weeks, 
and  had  taken  off*  with  him  several  essential  parts  of  her  machinery. 

After  some  search  Halligan  was  found  comfortably  established  in  the 
Battle  House,  and  Mr.  Walker,  by  energetic  and  good  management, 
has  recovered  from  him  the  necessary  machinery  and  thinks  he  can

[Capt.  Charles  H.  Allen,  a  4  ^  ^ 

Company  A,  Second  KentucTcy  Cavalry,  Acting  Adjutant. \ 

Captain:  In  obedience  to  instructions  from  Col.  John  S.  Scott,  ask-f 
ing  a  report  of  the  operations  and  condition  of  my  command,  1  have 
the  honor  to  submit  the  following  statement,  and  respectfully  ask 
attention  to  the  suggestions  hereinafter  mentioned:  Having  selected  ar 
encampment,  suitable  alike  for  foraging  my  command  and  for  the  arresi 
of  the  absentees  from  the  brigade,  I  ordered  detachments  from  ^e  Third 
and  Fifth  Regiments,  and  cavalry,  under  strict  and  vigilant  otocers,  ic 
scour  the  districts  where  my  men  most  frequented,  with  instructiom 
to  arrest  and  bring  to  camp,  closely  guarded,  all  absentees  from  the 
army  found  without  proper  and  legal  authority,  and  all  men  betweer 
the  ages  of  eighteen  and  forty-five.  Details  are  daily 
prisoners,  and  a  report  from  Lieutenant-Colonel  Amacker,  of  the  ihii 
Louisiana  Regiment,  gives  me  every  reason  to  believe  that  ^ojit 
ing  parties  are  rendering  efficient  and  long-needed  service.  Men  ha\ 
been  arrested  and  are  now  in  confinement  that  have  been  absent  wi 
out  leave  from  their  armies  from  twelve  to  eighteen  months,  roaming 
the  country  as  jayhawkers,  cotton- stealers  and  runners,  marauders 
ieopardizing  alike  the  discipline  of  the  army  and  the  safety  of  tin 
citizen.  These  men  have  attached  themselves  to  wild-cat  orpnizations 
and  under  a  partial  recognition  from  unauthorized  authority- ais 
trict  headquarters— have  for  a  time  baffled  every  attempt  in  return 
ing  them  to  duty.  These  organizations  have  had  my  especial  attentmn 
and  the  men  of  my  own  command,  and  all  others  found  in 
be  arrested  and  the  status  of  the  officers  examined.  I  am  conhuen 
that  within  six  weeks  this  entire  country,  which  might  be  styled  ru 
‘‘deserters’  home,”  can  be  thoroughly  cleaned  and  the  regiments  o 
the  brigade  filled  up  to  a  respectable  number.  My  attention  is  givei 
to  the  discipline  of  the  men  and  officers  in  camp  and  to  unpr 
ment  of  the  condition  of  my  horses,  sadly  reduced  by  late  ueav.
